specStatements.text: Students should be able to explain how the structure of the nervous system is adapted to its functions.
The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour.

Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system (CNS). The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
stimulus →receptor →coordinator →effector →response

Students should be able to explain how the various structures in a reflex arc – including the sensory neurone, synapse, relay neurone and motor neurone – relate to their function. Students should understand why reflex actions are important.
Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; they do not involve the conscious part of the brain.
Students should be able to extract and interpret data from graphs, charts and tables, about the functioning of the nervous system.
Students should be able to translate information about reaction times between numerical and graphical forms.
The brain controls complex behaviour. It is made of billions of interconnected neurones and has different regions that carry out different functions.
Students should be able to identify the cerebral cortex, cerebellum and medulla on a diagram of the brain, and describe their functions.
Students should be able to explain some of the difficulties of investigating brain function and treating brain damage and disease.

Neuroscientists have been able to map the regions of the brain to particular functions by studying patients with brain damage, electrically stimulating different parts of the brain and using MRI scanning techniques. The complexity and delicacy of the brain makes investigating and treating brain disorders very difficult.
Students should be able to relate the structures of the eye to their functions. This includes: accommodation to focus on near or distant objects; adaptation to dim light.
The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour.

Students should be able to identify the following structures on a diagram of the eye and explain how their structure is related to their function: retina; optic nerve; sclera; cornea; iris; ciliary muscles; suspensory ligaments.
Accommodation is the process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.
To focus on a near object: the ciliary muscles contract; the suspensory ligaments loosen; the lens is then thicker and refracts light rays strongly.
To focus on a distant object: the ciliary muscles relax; the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight; the lens is then pulled thin and only slightly refracts light rays.

Two common defects of the eyes are myopia (short sightedness) and hyperopia (long sightedness) in which rays of light do not focus on the retina. Generally these defects are treated with spectacle lenses which refract the light rays so that they do focus on the retina.; New technologies now include hard and soft contact lenses, laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea and a replacement lens in the eye.
Students should be able to interpret ray diagrams, showing these two common defects of the eye and demonstrate how spectacle lenses correct them.

Body temperature is monitored and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain. The thermoregulatory centre contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood. The skin contains temperature receptors and sends nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre.

If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands. Both these mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.
If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction), sweating stops and skeletal muscles contract (shiver).
Students should be able to explain how these mechanisms lower or raise body temperature in a given context.

concepts.definition: The system of receptors, neurones and the central nervous system that enables humans to react to their surroundings and to coordinate their behaviour.
A cell or structure that detects a stimulus, for example the light receptors in the retina or the temperature receptors in the skin.
A nerve cell that carries information as electrical impulses from receptors to the central nervous system, and from the central nervous system to effectors.
The brain and spinal cord. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors to the information it receives from receptors.
A structure that brings about the response. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
The sequence stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response, which describes how the body detects and responds to a change.
An automatic and rapid response to a stimulus that does not involve the conscious part of the brain.
The pathway taken by an impulse in a reflex action: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone in the CNS → motor neurone → effector.
The junction between two neurones. A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.
The organ that controls complex behaviour. It is made of billions of interconnected neurones and has different regions that carry out different functions.
The outer, folded region of the brain, responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.
The region at the back and base of the brain, responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance.
The region of the brain stem that controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.
The sclera is the tough white outer layer that protects the eye; the cornea is the transparent front part of that layer, which refracts light entering the eye.
The coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil, and so controls how much light enters the eye.
The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour; the optic nerve carries impulses from the retina to the brain.
A ring of muscle and the ligaments that attach it to the lens. Together they change the shape of the lens during accommodation.
The process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects.
A defect of the eye in which rays of light from a distant object focus in front of the retina. It is generally treated with a concave spectacle lens that makes the rays focus on the retina.
A defect of the eye in which rays of light focus behind the retina. It is generally treated with a convex spectacle lens that refracts the rays so that they focus on the retina.

Spectacle lenses refract light rays so that they focus on the retina. New technologies include hard and soft contact lenses, laser surgery to change the shape of the cornea, and a replacement lens in the eye.

The centre in the brain that monitors and controls body temperature. It contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood and receives nervous impulses from temperature receptors in the skin.
The widening of blood vessels supplying the skin when body temperature is too high, which, with sweat produced from the sweat glands, causes a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.
The narrowing of blood vessels supplying the skin when body temperature is too low, which reduces the transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.

misconceptions.question: In a response to a stimulus, which structure brings about the response?
misconceptions.correct: The effector brings about the response: a muscle contracting or a gland secreting a hormone. The receptor only detects the stimulus.
misconceptions.misconception: The structure that detects the stimulus is also the structure that brings about the response.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Detection and response often happen in the same part of the body, such as the hand touching something hot, so students merge the two roles into one structure.
misconceptions.correction: Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system. The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones, so receptor and effector are different structures in the pathway stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response.

misconceptions.question: Which parts of the nervous system make up the central nervous system?
misconceptions.correct: The brain and the spinal cord only.
misconceptions.misconception: The central nervous system includes all the nerves in the body, including those in the arms and legs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'nervous system' and 'central nervous system' are used loosely in everyday speech, and diagrams often show the brain, spinal cord and nerves in one colour.
misconceptions.correction: The CNS is the brain and spinal cord. Neurones carrying impulses from receptors to the CNS, and from the CNS to effectors, are not part of the CNS.

misconceptions.question: How does information pass from one neurone to the next at a synapse?
misconceptions.correct: A chemical is released and diffuses across the gap, setting off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.
misconceptions.misconception: The electrical impulse passes straight across the synapse from one neurone into the next.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that impulses are electrical and picture the reflex arc as one continuous wire, so the gap at the synapse is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: Impulses travel along neurones as electrical impulses, but at a synapse a chemical diffuses across the gap and starts a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

misconceptions.question: Does a reflex action involve the conscious part of the brain?
misconceptions.correct: No. Reflex actions are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain.
misconceptions.misconception: A reflex happens because the person decides very quickly to move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The person is usually awake and aware of what happened, and they notice the movement, so they assume they chose it.
misconceptions.correction: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; they do not involve the conscious part of the brain. Awareness of what happened comes after the response, not before it.

misconceptions.question: Does the impulse in a reflex arc pass through the central nervous system?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The impulse passes through a relay neurone in the CNS, even though the conscious part of the brain is not involved.
misconceptions.misconception: Because a reflex is not conscious, the impulse does not pass through the central nervous system at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students equate the CNS with conscious thought, so 'not conscious' is read as 'not in the brain or spinal cord'.
misconceptions.correction: In a reflex arc the sensory neurone passes the impulse across a synapse to a relay neurone in the CNS, which passes it on to the motor neurone. The CNS still coordinates the response; only the conscious part of the brain is not involved.

misconceptions.question: Which region of the brain controls heart rate and breathing rate?
misconceptions.correct: The medulla controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.
misconceptions.misconception: The cerebellum controls heart rate and breathing rate.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The cerebellum and medulla are both drawn low down and towards the back of a brain diagram, and both are linked with things we do not think about.
misconceptions.correction: The brain has different regions that carry out different functions: the cerebral cortex is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language; the cerebellum coordinates muscular activity and balance; the medulla controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.

misconceptions.question: Why is it difficult to investigate brain function and to treat brain damage and disease?
misconceptions.correct: The brain is extremely complex and delicate, and it is hard to reach without causing further damage.
misconceptions.misconception: Because MRI scanning shows the brain in such detail, damaged regions can be found and repaired straightforwardly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Detailed scan images look complete, so students assume that seeing a structure means it can be understood and repaired.
misconceptions.correction: Neuroscientists have mapped regions of the brain to particular functions by studying patients with brain damage, electrically stimulating different parts of the brain and using MRI scanning techniques, but the complexity and delicacy of the brain makes investigating and treating brain disorders very difficult.

misconceptions.question: What do the ciliary muscles do when the eye focuses on a near object?
misconceptions.correct: They contract, the suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens becomes thicker, so it refracts light rays strongly.
misconceptions.misconception: The ciliary muscles contract to focus on a distant object and relax to focus on a near object.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume that a contracting muscle must pull the suspensory ligaments tight, when contracting the ring of ciliary muscle actually makes the ring smaller and slackens the ligaments.
misconceptions.correction: To focus on a near object the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens is thicker. To focus on a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thin.

misconceptions.question: Which structure of the eye changes shape during accommodation?
misconceptions.correct: The lens changes shape during accommodation.
misconceptions.misconception: The cornea changes shape to focus light from near and distant objects.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The cornea does refract light entering the eye, and students hear that laser surgery changes the shape of the cornea, so they assume the cornea is what adjusts the focus.
misconceptions.correction: Accommodation is the process of changing the shape of the lens to focus on near or distant objects. The cornea refracts light entering the eye but does not change shape to focus it.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the pupil when a person moves into dim light?
misconceptions.correct: The iris muscles make the pupil wider, so more light enters the eye.
misconceptions.misconception: In dim light the pupil becomes narrower.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate narrowing the eyes with trying to see, and rarely watch a pupil change in a mirror as the light level falls.
misconceptions.correction: The eye adapts to dim light by the iris muscles widening the pupil, allowing more light to reach the receptors in the retina. In bright light the iris muscles narrow the pupil to protect the retina.

misconceptions.question: In myopia (short sightedness), where do rays of light from a distant object focus, and which lens corrects it?
misconceptions.correct: They focus in front of the retina, and a concave spectacle lens is used to make them focus on the retina.
misconceptions.misconception: In short sightedness rays of light focus behind the retina, and a convex spectacle lens is used to correct it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The names 'short' and 'long' sightedness are read as describing where the light lands rather than the distance at which the person can see clearly, so the two defects are swapped.
misconceptions.correction: In myopia rays of light focus in front of the retina and a concave spectacle lens spreads the rays out so that they focus on the retina. In hyperopia rays focus behind the retina and a convex spectacle lens refracts them more strongly so that they focus on the retina.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the blood vessels supplying the skin when body temperature is too high?
misconceptions.correct: They dilate (vasodilation), so more blood flows through the capillaries near the skin surface.
misconceptions.misconception: The blood vessels move closer to the surface of the skin.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook diagrams of hot and cold skin are often drawn with the vessels at different depths, which looks like movement rather than a change in width.
misconceptions.correction: If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands. Both these mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment. The vessels change width; they do not change position.

misconceptions.question: Which part of the body monitors and controls body temperature?
misconceptions.correct: The thermoregulatory centre in the brain monitors and controls body temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: The skin monitors and controls body temperature by itself, without the brain being involved.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sweating, shivering and changes in skin colour all happen in the skin, so students treat the skin as the control centre rather than as the place where the response happens.
misconceptions.correction: Body temperature is monitored and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain, which contains receptors sensitive to the temperature of the blood. The skin contains temperature receptors and sends nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre.

misconceptions.question: A student's mean reaction time falls from 0.30 s to 0.22 s after practice. What does this show?
misconceptions.correct: The student is reacting faster after practice, because a shorter time means a quicker response.
misconceptions.misconception: A larger reaction time value means a faster reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In most measurements a bigger number means 'more' or 'better', so a taller bar on a chart is read as a better performance.
misconceptions.correction: Reaction time is the time taken to respond, so the smaller the value the faster the response. On a bar chart or graph of reaction times, a lower bar or point shows the quicker reaction.

misconceptions.question: Can a gland be an effector?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.
misconceptions.misconception: Only muscles can act as effectors.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The examples used most often, such as pulling a hand away or shivering, all involve movement, so glands are forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: The CNS coordinates the response of effectors which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones, so a gland secreting a hormone is just as much an effector as a contracting muscle.

misconceptions.question: What causes shivering when body temperature is too low?
misconceptions.correct: Skeletal muscles contract rapidly (shiver) in response to impulses from the thermoregulatory centre.
misconceptions.misconception: Shivering is caused by the blood vessels in the skin narrowing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'constrict' and 'contract' sound alike, and both responses to cold are learned together, so students link them as cause and effect.
misconceptions.correction: If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction), sweating stops and skeletal muscles contract (shiver). These are separate responses coordinated by the thermoregulatory centre; vasoconstriction does not cause shivering.

misconceptions.question: One student's reaction time improves over three trials. What can be concluded from this?
misconceptions.correct: That this student's reaction time improved over these three trials.
misconceptions.misconception: A pattern in one person's results shows what would happen for other people too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are used to drawing a single conclusion from a practical, and a clear trend in a small table looks convincing on its own.
misconceptions.correction: Data extracted from a graph, chart or table describe the individuals actually measured. A conclusion about the functioning of the nervous system in other people needs data from those people as well.

mcqs.stem: A single neurone carries impulses from a receptor in the toe to the spinal cord. Which statement best explains how this structure is adapted to its function?

options.text: It is long, so impulses reach the CNS quickly.
options.rationale: Information from receptors passes along cells (neurones) as electrical impulses to the central nervous system, so one long cell carries the impulse the whole way to the spinal cord without delay.

options.text: It detects the stimulus and causes the response.
options.rationale: A student who believes the structure that detects a stimulus also produces the response treats the neurone as receptor and effector combined. In the pathway stimulus → receptor → coordinator → effector → response, the neurone only carries information; receptors detect and effectors respond.

options.text: It is part of the central nervous system.
options.rationale: A student who thinks all nerves belong to the CNS counts this neurone as part of it. The CNS is the brain and spinal cord, so a neurone running from the toe to the spinal cord is not part of the CNS.

options.text: It carries the impulse without using the CNS.
options.rationale: A student who believes rapid responses bypass the CNS assumes the neurone works alone. Information from receptors passes to the CNS, which coordinates the response of effectors.

mcqs.stem: Effectors in the human body may be:

options.text: muscles contracting or glands secreting
options.rationale: The CNS coordinates the response of effectors, which may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

options.text: receptors detecting light and sound levels
options.rationale: A student who merges the roles of receptor and effector picks the structure that detects the stimulus. Receptors detect stimuli; effectors bring about the response.

options.text: skeletal muscles moving bones at a joint
options.rationale: A student who believes only muscles can be effectors chooses an answer that leaves glands out. The specification states that effectors may be muscles contracting or glands secreting hormones.

options.text: neurones carrying impulses into the brain
options.rationale: A student who treats every neurone as part of the central nervous system confuses the cells that carry information with the structures that respond. Neurones carry impulses to the CNS, which then coordinates the response of effectors.

mcqs.stem: In a reflex arc, what is the function of the relay neurone?

options.text: It carries the impulse to the conscious brain.
options.rationale: A student who believes a reflex involves a quick decision looks for a route to the conscious brain. Reflex actions are automatic and rapid and do not involve the conscious part of the brain.

options.text: It links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone.
options.rationale: In a reflex arc the sensory neurone passes the impulse across a synapse to a relay neurone in the CNS, which passes it on to the motor neurone that carries the impulse to the effector.

options.text: It carries the electrical impulse across the synapse.
options.rationale: A student who pictures the reflex arc as one continuous electrical wire thinks a neurone bridges the synapse. At a synapse a chemical diffuses across the gap and sets off a new electrical impulse in the next neurone.

options.text: It carries the impulse from the skin without the CNS.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a reflex misses out the CNS altogether places the whole pathway in the limb. The relay neurone is in the CNS; it is the conscious part of the brain, not the CNS, that is not involved.

mcqs.stem: Why is a reflex action important when a person touches a very hot object?

options.text: It gives the person time to decide how to act.
options.rationale: A student who believes reflexes involve a fast decision sees thinking time as the benefit. Reflex actions do not involve the conscious part of the brain, and any decision would slow the response down.

options.text: It keeps the impulse out of the nervous system.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a reflex bypasses the CNS treats that as the reason it is fast. The impulse still passes through a relay neurone in the CNS; speed comes from not involving the conscious part of the brain.

options.text: It is automatic and rapid, so injury is reduced.
options.rationale: Reflex actions are automatic and rapid; the hand is moved away from the stimulus before the conscious part of the brain is involved, which limits the damage done.

options.text: It lets the receptor make the response itself.
options.rationale: A student who merges receptor and effector assumes the skin acts on its own. Receptors detect the stimulus and effectors, such as the muscles of the arm, bring about the response.

mcqs.stem: A table shows one student's mean reaction time in three trials: trial 1, 0.28 s; trial 2, 0.24 s; trial 3, 0.21 s. What do these data show?

options.text: The reaction time fell across the trials.
options.rationale: Reading the values in order from the table shows a decrease from 0.28 s to 0.21 s, which is the pattern the data support.

options.text: The reaction time rose across the trials.
options.rationale: A student who reads reaction time as a score rather than a time sees improvement as an increase. The values 0.28 s, 0.24 s and 0.21 s get smaller, so the reaction time fell.

options.text: The student reacted more slowly each time.
options.rationale: A student who believes a bigger number means a faster reaction reads a falling time as getting slower. Reaction time is the time taken to respond, so a smaller value means a quicker response.

options.text: The results apply to other students too.
options.rationale: A student who generalises from one person extends the trend to everyone. These data come from one student in three trials and describe only that student.

mcqs.stem: Four students have mean reaction times of 0.15 s, 0.22 s, 0.28 s and 0.31 s. These values are drawn as a bar chart. Which statement about the chart is correct?

options.text: The tallest bar is the fastest time.
options.rationale: A student who reads a taller bar as a better performance picks this. The tallest bar shows the longest reaction time, which is the slowest response.

options.text: The shortest bar is the slowest time.
options.rationale: A student who thinks a larger value means a faster reaction reads the shortest bar as the worst result. The shortest bar, 0.15 s, is the shortest time and so the fastest reaction.

options.text: The tallest bar is the 0.31 s time.
options.rationale: Translating the numbers into graphical form, bar height is proportional to reaction time, so the largest value, 0.31 s, gives the tallest bar.

options.text: Each bar stands for the whole group.
options.rationale: A student who does not separate individual results from group results treats one bar as representing everyone. Each bar shows the mean reaction time of one named student.

mcqs.stem: A patient can no longer coordinate their movements or keep their balance after an injury to the brain. Which is the most likely cause?

options.text: Damage within the medulla
options.rationale: A student who swaps the functions of the cerebellum and medulla chooses this. The medulla controls unconscious activities such as heart rate and breathing rate.

options.text: The cerebellum is damaged
options.rationale: The cerebellum is the region of the brain responsible for coordinating muscular activity and balance, which are the functions the patient has lost.

options.text: Cerebral cortex is damaged
options.rationale: A student who is unsure which region does which job picks the largest one. The cerebral cortex is responsible for consciousness, intelligence, memory and language.

options.text: Damage to the spinal cord
options.rationale: A student who does not distinguish the parts of the CNS chooses the spinal cord. The question describes damage within the brain, and it is the brain that has different regions carrying out different functions.

mcqs.stem: Neuroscientists want to find out which region of a patient's brain controls speech. Which statement explains why this is difficult?

options.text: Damaged brain regions are simple to repair.
options.rationale: A student who thinks modern medicine can repair the brain like other organs picks this. The complexity and delicacy of the brain makes treating brain disorders very difficult, and it does not explain the difficulty of investigating function.

options.text: MRI scanning shows which cells are working.
options.rationale: A student who assumes a detailed scan removes all uncertainty picks this. MRI scanning has helped map regions of the brain to particular functions, but it does not show the activity of individual neurones.

options.text: Each region of the brain does the same job.
options.rationale: A student who muddles the functions of the cerebellum, medulla and cerebral cortex may treat the regions as interchangeable. The brain has different regions that carry out different functions, which is why neuroscientists map them.

options.text: The brain is complex and easily damaged.
options.rationale: The brain is made of billions of interconnected neurones, and its complexity and delicacy make investigating brain function and treating brain damage and disease very difficult.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly relates a structure of the eye to its function?

options.text: The cornea changes shape to focus images.
options.rationale: A student who believes the cornea adjusts the focus picks this. The cornea refracts light entering the eye, but accommodation is the changing of the shape of the lens.

options.text: The iris narrows the pupil in dim lighting.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the pupil narrows when it is dark picks this. The iris does control pupil size, but in dim light the pupil is widened so that more light reaches the retina.

options.text: The ciliary muscles relax for near objects.
options.rationale: A student who swaps the near and distant responses picks this. To focus on a near object the ciliary muscles contract; they relax to focus on a distant object.

options.text: The retina contains receptors for light.
options.rationale: The eye is a sense organ containing receptors sensitive to light intensity and colour, and these receptors are found in the retina at the back of the eye.

mcqs.stem: A person walks out of bright sunlight into a dark room. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The iris muscles make the pupil narrower.
options.rationale: A student who links narrowing with trying to see picks this. Narrowing the pupil lets in less light, which is the response to bright light, not to dim light.

options.text: The ciliary muscles make the lens thicker.
options.rationale: A student who confuses accommodation with adaptation to dim light picks this. Changing the shape of the lens focuses light from near or distant objects; it does not control how much light enters the eye.

options.text: The cornea changes shape to admit light.
options.rationale: A student who believes the cornea changes shape applies that idea to light levels. The cornea refracts light entering the eye and keeps its shape; the iris controls the amount of light entering.

options.text: The iris muscles make the pupil wider.
options.rationale: The eye adapts to dim light by the iris muscles widening the pupil, so more light enters the eye and reaches the receptors in the retina.

mcqs.stem: A student looks up from a book and focuses on a tree in the distance. What happens in the eye?

options.text: The ciliary muscles contract and the lens thickens.
options.rationale: A student who swaps the near and distant responses picks this. Contracting ciliary muscles and a thicker lens are used to focus on a near object, such as the book.

options.text: The suspensory ligaments loosen and the lens bulges.
options.rationale: A student who thinks loose ligaments go with distant vision picks this. The suspensory ligaments loosen for a near object; for a distant object they are pulled tight.

options.text: The cornea changes shape and the lens stays thin.
options.rationale: A student who believes the cornea does the focusing picks this. Accommodation is the process of changing the shape of the lens, not the cornea.

options.text: The ciliary muscles relax and the lens is pulled thin.
options.rationale: To focus on a distant object the ciliary muscles relax, the suspensory ligaments are pulled tight and the lens is pulled thin, so it only slightly refracts the light rays.

mcqs.stem: A ray diagram shows light from a distant object coming to a focus in front of the retina. Which defect is shown, and how is it corrected?

options.text: Myopia, corrected with a convex lens.
options.rationale: A student who identifies the defect from the diagram but pairs it with the wrong lens picks this. A convex lens refracts the rays more strongly and would bring the focus even further in front of the retina.

options.text: Hyperopia, corrected with a convex lens.
options.rationale: A student who has the two defects swapped reads the diagram as long sightedness. In hyperopia the rays focus behind the retina, not in front of it.

options.text: Myopia, corrected with a concave lens.
options.rationale: Rays focusing in front of the retina show myopia (short sightedness); a concave spectacle lens spreads the rays out so that they do focus on the retina.

options.text: Hyperopia, corrected with a concave lens.
options.rationale: A student who swaps the defects but remembers the lens for a focus in front of the retina picks this. The lens is right for the diagram shown, but the defect is myopia, not hyperopia.

mcqs.stem: A person is exercising hard and their body temperature rises above normal. What happens in the skin?

options.text: Blood vessels dilate and sweat is produced.
options.rationale: If the body temperature is too high, blood vessels dilate (vasodilation) and sweat is produced from the sweat glands; both mechanisms cause a transfer of energy from the skin to the environment.

options.text: Blood vessels move nearer the skin surface.
options.rationale: A student who reads hot and cold skin diagrams as showing vessels at different depths picks this. The blood vessels dilate, changing their width, but they do not change position.

options.text: Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
options.rationale: A student who links narrowing vessels with shivering applies the cold response here. Vasoconstriction and shivering occur when body temperature is too low, and they reduce energy transfer from the skin.

options.text: The skin cools the body without the brain.
options.rationale: A student who treats the skin as the control centre picks this. Body temperature is monitored and controlled by the thermoregulatory centre in the brain, which the skin's temperature receptors send impulses to.

mcqs.stem: A person waits at a bus stop in cold weather and their body temperature begins to fall. How does the body raise it again?

options.text: Blood vessels dilate and shivering begins.
options.rationale: A student who is unsure which way the vessels change picks this. Vasodilation increases the transfer of energy from the skin to the environment, which would cool the body further.

options.text: Blood vessels constrict and shivering starts.
options.rationale: If the body temperature is too low, blood vessels constrict (vasoconstriction) and sweating stops, reducing energy transfer from the skin, while skeletal muscles contract (shiver), releasing energy that warms the body.

options.text: Narrowing blood vessels cause the shivering.
options.rationale: A student who confuses 'constrict' with 'contract' treats one response as the cause of the other. Vasoconstriction and shivering are separate responses coordinated by the thermoregulatory centre.

options.text: The skin warms the blood without using the brain.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the skin controls body temperature itself picks this. The skin's temperature receptors send nervous impulses to the thermoregulatory centre in the brain, which coordinates the response.
